title.value: Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning
title.justification: The title is explicitly mentioned several times, such as in the introduction and figure descriptions.
title.quote: Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning

analysis.description: The paper presents a method called SCoRe, which uses reinforcement learning to improve the self-correction capabilities of large language models (LLMs). The novel approach addresses distribution shift and behavior collapse in previous supervised fine-tuning methods by training on self-generated data, enhancing model performance on reasoning tasks such as MATH and HumanEval.

type.justification: The paper is empirical because it includes experimentation and quantitative evaluation on tasks like MATH and HumanEval to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed SCoRe method.
type.quote: Our main contribution is SCoRe, a multi-turn RL approach for teaching LLMs how to correct their own mistakes. To the best of our knowledge, SCoRe is the first approach to attain significantly positive intrinsic self-correction.

name.justification: The primary focus of the paper is enhancing the capabilities of large language models through self-correction, a key task in Natural Language Processing.
name.quote: Self-correction is a highly desirable capability of large language models (LLMs)... we study a special instance of training LLMs to perform self-correction to fix their mistakes “on-the-fly”.

name.justification: The paper utilizes reinforcement learning as the core method for improving self-correction capabilities in language models.
name.quote: To develop SCoRe, we start by analyzing the shortcomings of SFT-based approaches (e.g., STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022)) and naïve RL that optimizes final response correctness for teaching self-correction.

name.justification: Mathematical problem solving is a test field used to evaluate the self-correction capabilities of the refined language models.
name.quote: Relative to base Gemini models, our method attains an absolute 15.6% gain on self-correction for reasoning problems from MATH...

name.justification: The paper uses Gemini 1.0 Pro as one of the base models to evaluate the self-correction capability improvement through SCoRe.
name.quote: With Gemini 1.0 Pro and 1.5 Flash models, we find that SCoRe achieves state-of-the-art self-correction performance.

is_contributed.justification: The model itself is not contributed by the paper; rather, it is used as part of the experimental setup to test SCoRe.
is_contributed.quote: For all of our experiments on coding problems, we fine-tune Gemini 1.0 Pro and for MATH, we fine-tune Gemini 1.5 Flash.

is_executed.justification: The model was actively executed as part of the experiments to demonstrate the efficacy of SCoRe.
is_executed.quote: For all of our experiments on coding problems, we fine-tune Gemini 1.0 Pro and for MATH, we fine-tune Gemini 1.5 Flash.

is_compared.justification: The paper provides comparative results showing improvements in self-correction using Gemini models enhanced with SCoRe.
is_compared.quote: Relative to the base model Gemini 1.5 Flash, SCoRe improves Δ (t1, t2) by 15.6%, and Accuracy@t2 by 23.0%, and over the next best prior approach, Pair-SFT, by 10.2% and 2.6% respectively.
